title: The garden of Eden
note: Genesis names four rivers, and two of them — the Tigris and Euphrates — are real and known. The other two, Pishon and Gihon, cannot be identified with any confidence, and no site has ever been agreed on.

title: The ark comes to rest
note: The Bible says 'the mountains of Ararat' — a whole region (ancient Urartu), not one peak. The pin is on Mount Ararat, the peak that later tradition settled on, but the text does not name it.

title: The tower of Babel
note: Most scholars connect the story with Babylon and its great ziggurat, Etemenanki, whose ruins are pinned here. The link is very widely held but the text itself only says 'a plain in Shinar'.

title: Abraham leaves Ur
note: The great Sumerian city of Ur, excavated by Leonard Woolley. A minority argue for a northern Ur near Urfa in Turkey, but the southern site is the standard identification.

title: Abraham settles in Haran
note: A real, continuously known town on the trade route between Mesopotamia and Canaan. Its beehive mudbrick houses still stand.

title: Abraham arrives in Canaan
place: Shechem, by the oak of Moreh
note: Tell Balata has been excavated and matches Shechem's description in the text and in Egyptian records.

title: Sodom and Gomorrah
note: Somewhere near the Dead Sea, almost certainly, but that is as far as agreement goes.

title: Abraham and Isaac on the mountain
note: 2 Chronicles 3:1 links Moriah with the temple hill in Jerusalem, which is where the pin sits. The Samaritan tradition places it on Mount Gerizim instead.

title: Abraham buys a burial cave
note: One of the oldest continuously venerated sites anywhere. The Herodian enclosure above the cave still stands.

title: Jacob's dream of the stairway
note: Beitin preserves the ancient name and fits the distances given in the Bible. A minority propose nearby el-Bireh.

title: Jacob wrestles until daybreak
place: Peniel, at the ford of the Jabbok
note: The river is certain — the Jabbok is today's Zarqa. Which ford, and where Peniel itself stood, is not settled; the leading candidate for the town is Tulul adh-Dhahab, about 7km upstream. The pin marks the river crossing area.

title: Joseph is sold by his brothers
note: Excavated and securely identified, on the caravan route that ran down to Egypt — exactly the road the traders in the story were taking.

title: Joseph rules in Egypt
note: The Bible never names the pharaoh or his capital, and Egypt's capital moved several times. Memphis and Avaris are both suggested; neither can be confirmed.

title: The burning bush
note: The same mountain as Sinai, and just as unlocated. Tradition points to Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai; other scholars argue for northern Sinai or even Arabia.

title: Crossing the sea
note: The Hebrew reads 'Sea of Reeds', which does not clearly mean the Red Sea. Proposed crossings run from the Bitter Lakes to the Gulf of Suez to the Gulf of Aqaba.

title: The Ten Commandments
note: Despite the monastery, the tour buses and fifteen centuries of tradition, no one can demonstrate which mountain this was.

title: The twelve spies report back
note: Tell el-Qudeirat has the largest spring in the area and is the leading candidate, but the identification rests on geography rather than an inscription.

title: Moses sees the land he cannot enter
note: The view from the summit — Jericho, the Jordan valley, Jerusalem's hills on a clear day — matches the text closely. Venerated since at least the 4th century.

title: Israel crosses the Jordan
note: The text says 'opposite Jericho', which narrows it to a few kilometres of river. This pin marks the traditional ford.

title: The walls of Jericho fall
note: One of the oldest walled towns on earth and beyond doubt as a location. Archaeologists argue hard about the dating of its destruction — but not about where it is.

title: The day the sun stood still
note: Jar handles stamped 'Gibeon' were found at the site, which is about as direct as archaeological confirmation gets.

title: Blessings and curses on two mountains
note: Both mountains are known and stand either side of the valley at Shechem. The pin is on Gerizim; Ebal is the taller peak opposite.

title: Deborah and Barak
note: A distinctive dome of a hill rising alone out of the Jezreel valley — unmistakable, then and now.

title: Gideon's three hundred
note: The spring at the foot of Mount Gilboa, where Gideon watched how his men drank.

title: Samson and the gates of Gaza
note: One of the five Philistine cities, occupied continuously since. The temple of Dagon he pulled down has never been found.

title: Ruth gleans in the fields
note: The town is certain. Which fields Boaz owned is not, but they lay in the valleys just east of the town.

title: God calls the boy Samuel
note: Israel's worship centre before Jerusalem, and securely identified. Excavation has found a large storage complex from exactly this period.

title: The ark in the temple of Dagon
note: A major Philistine city, excavated and well identified. The ancient tell sits a few kilometres from the modern city.

title: David and Goliath
note: The text names Socoh and Azekah on either side, and both are identified — so the valley between them is fixed with unusual precision.

title: David spares Saul in the cave
note: The oasis is certain and still spectacular. Which of its many caves is anyone's guess.

title: Saul and the woman of Endor
note: The general area between Mount Tabor and the Hill of Moreh, to its south-west, is agreed. The precise site is not — at least five ruins in that basin have been proposed. The pin sits on the most commonly marked of them.

title: Saul dies on the mountain
note: The ridge overlooking the Jezreel valley, subject of David's lament: 'How the mighty have fallen.'

title: David captures Jerusalem
note: The original Jebusite city sat on the narrow spur south of the Temple Mount — much smaller than most people picture. It is heavily excavated.

title: Solomon builds the temple
note: The platform is certain. Nothing of Solomon's building survives above ground, and the site cannot be excavated.

title: The Queen of Sheba visits Solomon
note: Sheba is usually placed in southern Arabia — modern Yemen — but Ethiopian tradition claims her, and the kingdom's borders are unclear. Her visit takes place in Jerusalem; her home does not.

title: Elijah and the prophets of Baal
note: The mountain range is certain. This pin is the traditional spot at its south-eastern end, which fits the story's details — a view of the sea, and a run down to Jezreel — but is tradition, not proof.

title: Naboth's vineyard
note: Ahab's royal compound — a chariot base and second residence, with Samaria as the capital. Excavated in the 1990s. A large rock-cut winery has been found at the foot of the tell; the excavators date it to the Iron Age, though installations cut straight into bedrock are hard to date.

title: Chariots of fire around Elisha
note: The same hill where Joseph was sold, centuries earlier. Excavated and securely identified.

title: The fall of Samaria
note: The capital of the northern kingdom, on a hill with commanding views. Extensively excavated; the Assyrian conquest is recorded on their side too.

title: Hezekiah's tunnel
note: You can still walk through it, in the water. An inscription cut by the tunnellers describing the moment the two teams met was found inside.

title: Jerusalem falls; the exile begins
note: Both ends of this story are known places. The Babylonian Chronicle records the earlier capture of the city in 597 BC, but breaks off before the final destruction — for that, the evidence is the burnt destruction layer in the City of David and the ration tablets naming the exiled king Jehoiachin in Babylon.

title: Daniel in Babylon
note: The city is one of the best known sites in the ancient world. The lions' den and the fiery furnace are not marked anywhere in it.

title: Esther in the palace
note: The Persian palace at Susa has been excavated, and its columned hall and garden courts fit the kind of setting the book describes.

title: Nehemiah rebuilds the walls
note: A stretch of wall on the eastern slope has been identified by some excavators as Nehemiah's, though that particular claim is argued over.

title: Jeremiah buys a field
note: Jeremiah's home village, a few kilometres north-east of Jerusalem. Three sites within about a kilometre of each other have been proposed; the modern village of Anata, where the pin sits, preserves the name and has produced pottery of the right period.

title: Ezekiel's vision by the river
note: The Kebar is generally identified with a canal near Nippur named in Babylonian records. The pin is on Nippur; the canal's exact course is uncertain.

title: Jonah preaches to Nineveh
note: The Assyrian capital, its walls and palaces excavated since the 1840s. Tarshish, the port Jonah fled towards, is the unknown half of this story.

title: The land of Uz
note: Somewhere east or south-east of Israel — Edom and northern Arabia are both suggested. The book is deliberately vague about it.

title: The angel visits Mary
note: A small farming village of perhaps a few hundred people in Jesus' day. First-century houses and a wine press have been excavated beneath the modern city.

title: Jesus is born
note: The town is certain. The pin is the Church of the Nativity, built over a cave that was already being pointed out as the birthplace by the 2nd century — early, but tradition all the same.

title: The shepherds and the angels
note: The grazing land east of Bethlehem is the right kind of place, and this pin marks the traditional field. There are two rival 'shepherds' fields' a few hundred metres apart.

title: The wise men and King Herod
note: The pin marks Herod's palace beside today's Jaffa Gate, partly excavated, where the wise men would have been received. Bethlehem, six miles south, is where they found the child. Where they came from — "the east" — is unknown.

title: The escape to Egypt
note: The Bible says only 'Egypt'. Coptic tradition traces a detailed route with many stops, but none of it can be verified.

title: The boy Jesus in the temple
note: Herod's temple platform survives — the Western Wall is part of its retaining wall. The teaching would have happened in the porticoes around the courts.

title: Jesus is baptised
note: Al-Maghtas on the Jordanian bank is a UNESCO site with Byzantine churches built to mark the spot, and is the leading candidate. Qasr al-Yahud opposite makes the same claim.

title: Tempted in the wilderness
note: The Judean desert is a real and specific landscape, but no location is given. The cliff called the Mount of Temptation above Jericho is later tradition.

title: Water into wine
note: Two sites compete: Kafr Kanna, which has the churches and the tour buses, and Khirbet Qana a few kilometres north, which many archaeologists prefer. The pin is on Kafr Kanna.

title: Rejected in his home town
note: The town is certain; the synagogue building has not been found. The cliff the crowd dragged him to is traditionally the Mount of Precipice just south of the town.

title: Jesus makes Capernaum his base
note: Excavated in detail: the basalt houses, the fishing harbour, and a limestone synagogue standing on earlier basalt walls that many excavators read as the first-century synagogue. The best-attested place in the gospels.

title: Calling the first disciples
place: The shore of the Sea of Galilee
note: The lake and the fishing villages along its north shore are certain. A first-century fishing boat pulled from the mud in 1986 is on display nearby.

title: The Sermon on the Mount
note: The gospel says only 'a mountainside'. This hillside above Tabgha has been the traditional spot since the Byzantine period, and the acoustics genuinely work.

title: Healing at the pool
note: Excavated beside St Anne's Church, with the five porticoes John describes — a detail once used to argue the gospel was unreliable, until the pools were dug up.

title: The woman at the well
note: One of the few gospel sites that is a fixed physical object rather than a general area. The well is 40 metres deep and still gives water.

title: Feeding the five thousand
note: Luke says near Bethsaida, on the north-east shore; the traditional church is at Tabgha on the north-west shore. The pin follows tradition, but the two are several kilometres apart.

title: Walking on the water
note: The lake is the location, and the pin sits out on the open water. The sudden squalls the gospels describe are a real feature of it, funnelled down from the Golan.

title: The man among the tombs
note: The manuscripts disagree — Gerasenes, Gadarenes, Gergesenes. Kursi is the only candidate on the lake shore with a steep bank running into the water, and has a Byzantine monastery marking the spot.

title: Jairus' daughter and the woman in the crowd
note: Jairus was a synagogue leader. Capernaum's synagogue site is known — white limestone ruins standing on black basalt walls that most excavators take to be the earlier building.

title: 'Who do you say I am?'
note: A spring gushing from a cliff face lined with pagan shrines — including a cave once called the gate of the underworld. Jesus chose this spot to talk about the rock and the gates of Hades.

title: The transfiguration
note: Tabor is the traditional site and carries the churches. Many scholars prefer Mount Hermon, which is genuinely high and much nearer Caesarea Philippi, where the previous scene happens.

title: The road the Good Samaritan travelled
note: The parable is a story, not a report — but the road is real, and notoriously dangerous. The pin marks the traditional 'Inn of the Good Samaritan' at the halfway point.

title: Lazarus is raised
note: John puts it fifteen stadia from Jerusalem — under two miles — on the far side of the Mount of Olives, which fits exactly. The Arabic name al-Eizariya means "place of Lazarus".

title: Zacchaeus in the tree
note: New Testament Jericho was a separate town from the old tell, built around Herod's winter palace at the mouth of the Wadi Qelt. Both sites are known; this pin is on the New Testament one.

title: Blind Bartimaeus
note: On the main pilgrim road up to Jerusalem — the reason a beggar would sit there in the first place. The pin is on New Testament Jericho, around Herod's winter palace.

title: The entry into Jerusalem
place: From Bethphage over the Mount of Olives
note: The route is fixed by geography: over the ridge, and the whole city opens up in front of you at once. That view is still there.

title: Turning over the tables
note: The outer court was a vast open plaza — the money changers' tables would have stood near the southern entrance steps, which have been excavated.

title: The Last Supper
note: The gospels do not say where the room was. The building on Mount Zion has carried the tradition since the Byzantine period, but the room you can visit is medieval.

title: Gethsemane
note: An olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron valley from the temple. The area is certain; the exact plot is tradition, and four different churches keep rival gardens within a few hundred metres. Some of the olive trees are over 900 years old.

title: Peter denies Jesus
note: The house of Caiaphas has not been identified with certainty. This church on the eastern slope of Mount Zion is the traditional site and sits beside a first-century stepped street.

title: The trial before Pilate
note: Two candidates: the Antonia fortress beside the temple, where the Via Dolorosa begins, or Herod's palace near today's Jaffa Gate. Most historians now favour the palace, and that is where this pin sits — but the older tradition points across the city.

title: The crucifixion
place: Golgotha, the place of the skull
modern: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem
note: The Holy Sepulchre is the strong favourite: it was an abandoned quarry with tombs, outside the city wall of the time, and the tradition runs back to the 4th century. The Garden Tomb, popular since the 1800s, has little going for it archaeologically.

title: The empty tomb
place: The garden tomb of Joseph of Arimathea
modern: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem
note: Same site as Golgotha — John says the tomb was in a garden right beside the place of crucifixion. First-century rock-cut tombs survive inside the church, which supports the identification.

title: The road to Emmaus
note: Luke gives a distance — about seven miles from Jerusalem — and manuscripts disagree even on that. Four different villages claim it and none can prove it.

title: Breakfast on the shore
place: The shore of the Sea of Galilee
note: John says only "the Sea of Tiberias". Tabgha is the traditional spot, and a flat rock inside the little church there is shown as the table of Christ — a tradition running back to the 4th century, though the early accounts are not clear which rock they meant.

title: The ascension
place: The Mount of Olives, near Bethany
note: Acts names the Mount of Olives and gives the distance back to the city. The exact summit point is marked by a small domed chapel, which is tradition.

title: Pentecost
note: The city is certain; the house is not. The crowd Peter addressed would have gathered near the temple, where thousands were in the city for the festival.

title: Stephen is stoned
note: Executions took place outside the walls. Two traditions compete — one north of the city, one at the eastern gate now called St Stephen's Gate, which is where the pin sits.

title: Philip and the Ethiopian official
note: Acts says 'the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza'. There were several such roads and no specific spot is given.

title: Saul is stopped on the road
note: The city is certain, and Straight Street — where Saul stayed afterwards — still runs through the old city. The point on the road where it happened is not known.

title: Peter's vision on the roof
note: An ancient port, continuously occupied. The house of Simon the tanner is traditionally shown near the harbour, which is tradition rather than evidence.

title: Peter and Cornelius
note: Herod's harbour city, extensively excavated — theatre, aqueduct, and an inscription bearing Pontius Pilate's name. This is where the gospel first reaches a Roman household.

title: First called Christians
note: The third city of the Roman empire and the launch pad for Paul's journeys. Much of the ancient city lies under the modern one.

title: Paul's first mission: Cyprus
note: The Roman provincial capital of Cyprus, where Paul met the governor Sergius Paulus. The archaeological park is open to visitors.

title: Mistaken for gods at Lystra
note: Identified by an inscribed Roman altar found at the mound in 1885 naming the colony. Timothy came from here.

title: The Jerusalem council
note: The meeting that decided non-Jewish believers did not have to become Jews first. The city is certain; the meeting place is not recorded.

title: Lydia, and the earthquake in the jail
note: A Roman colony, well excavated — forum, theatre, and the riverside outside the gate where Acts says the women met to pray. The first church in Europe.

title: Trouble in Thessalonica
note: A major port, continuously a city ever since. Luke calls its officials 'politarchs' — an unusual title confirmed by inscriptions found there.

title: The Bereans check the scriptures
note: A quiet inland town then and a working city now, with a monument marking Paul's visit.

title: Paul at the Areopagus
note: The bare rock outcrop below the Acropolis where the council met. You can walk up it; Paul's speech is on a bronze plaque at the foot.

title: Eighteen months in Corinth
note: The bema — the public platform where Paul was hauled before Gallio — has been excavated and is still there. An inscription dates Gallio's term, which anchors Paul's whole timeline.

title: The riot of the silversmiths
note: One of the best preserved ancient cities anywhere. The theatre where the crowd chanted for two hours seats 24,000 and is still standing.

title: Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders
note: A great harbour city in Paul's day; the coastline has since silted up and the ruins now sit inland.

title: Paul on trial before Felix and Agrippa
note: Paul was held here for two years. The governor's palace on the promontory, where the hearings took place, has been excavated.

title: Shipwrecked on Malta
note: The island is named in the text and is not in doubt. Which bay the ship broke up in is — St Paul's Bay carries the tradition, and that is where the pin sits, but other bays fit the sailing directions better.

title: Paul reaches Rome
note: Acts ends with Paul under house arrest, still preaching. The Appian Way he entered the city on is still walkable.

title: John's visions on Patmos
note: A small Aegean island named directly in the text. The cave shown as the place of the visions is tradition, but the island is not in doubt.

title: The letters to the seven churches
note: All seven are named and all seven have been located: Ephesus, Smyrna (Izmir), Pergamum, Thyatira (Akhisar), Sardis, Philadelphia (Alaşehir) and Laodicea. The pin is on Sardis, roughly at the centre of the circuit.

title: The Syrophoenician woman
place: The region of Tyre and Sidon
note: Both cities are ancient, continuously occupied and certain. Jesus went outside Jewish territory here — that is the point of the story.

title: Healing the blind man at Bethsaida
note: The home town of Peter, Andrew and Philip. Two nearby sites both claim it — et-Tell on the hill and el-Araj by the shore — and excavation continues at both.

title: Jesus travels through Samaria
note: Sychar is usually identified with the village of Askar beside Jacob's well, though some argue it is Shechem itself, a little further west.

title: Naaman washes in the Jordan
note: The river is certain; the stretch he washed in is not recorded. The pin sits on the middle Jordan, between Galilee and the Dead Sea.

title: Solomon's fleet
note: The head of the Gulf of Aqaba is certain from the text. The pin is Tell el-Kheleifeh, the leading candidate — but excavation there has found nothing from Solomon's period, and the island of Jezirat Faraun is the main rival.

title: Mount Hermon
note: The snow-capped mountain at Israel's northern edge, named repeatedly as a boundary marker and never in doubt.

title: Beersheba, the southern edge
note: 'From Dan to Beersheba' was the standard way of saying 'the whole country'. The tell has an excavated well and a reconstructed horned altar.

title: Dan, the northern edge
note: The Tel Dan inscription found here mentions the 'House of David' — the earliest reference to David outside the Bible.

title: Megiddo, and Armageddon
note: A fortress city guarding the main pass into the Jezreel valley, with more than twenty cities stacked on top of each other. 'Armageddon' means 'mountain of Megiddo'.

title: The siege of Lachish
note: The one Bible siege we can see from the other side: Sennacherib carved the whole assault in stone for his palace at Nineveh, and the reliefs are in the British Museum.

title: Elijah runs for his life
note: Beersheba, where Elijah left his servant, is certain — the pin sits there. Where he walked for forty days afterwards, and which mountain he reached, is not: it is the same unlocated Horeb as in Exodus.

title: Isaac digs the wells
note: Tel Haror is the leading candidate for Gerar and fits the region described, but the identification is not certain.

title: David is made king at Hebron
note: David ruled here for seven years before taking Jerusalem. The town has been continuously occupied since the Bronze Age.

title: Samuel judges Israel at Mizpah
note: Two candidates: Tell en-Nasbeh, where the pin sits, and Nebi Samwil a few kilometres south. Most archaeologists favour Tell en-Nasbeh.

title: The vision of the man from Macedonia
note: The port where Paul turned west into Europe. The ruins, including a large bath complex, lie in the fields near the coast.

title: Paul preaches in the synagogue
note: A different Antioch from the Syrian one — a Roman colony up on the Anatolian plateau. Excavated, with a preserved aqueduct and theatre.

title: The letter to the Colossians
note: The mound is identified and visible. It sat unexcavated for a century; Turkish archaeologists began digging in 2021 and have since uncovered a large rock-cut necropolis on the slope below the city.

title: Phoebe's church at Cenchreae
note: Corinth's eastern port. The submerged harbour moles are still visible in the shallow water.
